prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision measurement of time and frequency

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest case on this shortlist of a basic quantum idea (the magic-wavelength lattice, which removes Doppler and recoil shifts while allowing many atoms to be interrogated at once) turning into a controllable device that made a new regime of physics measurable. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, tests of constant variation and dark-matter searches, and the coming redefinition of the second all follow from it. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST), so it is robust in precisely the sense I care about. The attribution is also tidy: Katori for the concept and first Sr lattice clocks, Ye for taking accuracy, stability and many-body clock physics to the frontier. Opening support is also the broadest on the list, with five top-three rankings and all eight members ranking it, including three first places.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier metrology prizes (Hall and Haensch 2005 for combs, Wineland 2012 for ion control). A sceptic can call the lattice clock an incremental, if spectacular, improvement in the same tradition rather than a new discovery. Credit is also not exclusive: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and ion-clock groups (Al+ and others) contributed to the broader story, and the thorium-229 nuclear clock or the formal redefinition of the second might later shift the natural configuration. Finally, I am an interested theorist in a neighbouring field, and my enthusiasm for clean controllable quantum systems may make me overrate this relative to discoveries with a more obviously new phenomenon.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B042 first but warns that overlap with the earlier metrology prizes (Hall and Haensch, Wineland) may weigh against it, and that a third contributor is not settled by the supplied credit.
responses.response: I agree the overlap is the main risk and I think it should be argued directly rather than waved away. The 2005 prize recognised combs and the 2012 prize recognised single-ion quantum control; neither covers trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that motional and recoil shifts vanish, which is what permits the 1e-18 stability and the many-body clock regime. On the third name, I would not add anyone: a two-person prize splits cleanly between concept and first demonstration (Katori) and accuracy frontier (Ye), and a third name would reopen the Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow question without a principled stopping point.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B056 first and B042 second, noting that the relation to earlier frequency-metrology prizes could lead some to see lattice clocks as incremental, and that it is unresolved whether Ye is better credited here or elsewhere.
responses.response: I take the incrementality worry seriously, but I would separate it from the question of whether a new regime opened. Going from the 1e-15 range to 1e-18 changed what can be done with a clock: relativistic geodesy at the millimetre scale, tests of fundamental constants, and a plausible redefinition of the second. On Ye, I see no real competition for his credit on this list; his lattice-clock work is distinct from the 2005 comb prize. I also respect B056 as a genuinely enabling instrument, but a prize on electron-optics correction would be judged on physics discovered with it, and I would defer to you on whether that bar is met.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B007 (topological insulators) first and B010 second, valuing a simple general mechanism with broad consequences, and ranks B042 last among his eight (rank 8).
responses.response: I understand the appeal of a Z2 invariant with a rigorous structure, and B007 is conceptually deeper than a clock in a narrow sense. But I would ask what the qualitative difference is in terms of reproducibility and a settled attribution: the topological-insulator trio leaves Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore and Hasan outside the credited names, and Haldane's 2016 prize already took part of the conceptual ground. The clock case has the same overlap issue with earlier prizes but a much cleaner attribution. I defer to you on the condensed-matter detail; if the committee thinks the allocation for B007 can be settled, I would see it as the strongest alternative together with B010.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B054 (magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene) first, as a theory-meets-experiment story that opened the moire-materials field, with Bistritzer a less natural third laureate.
responses.response: I ranked B054 seventh, and my disagreement is about maturity, not importance. The correlated phases are reproduced by many groups, but you yourself note that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and twist-angle disorder complicates reproducibility, so the interpretation is still moving. I agree with you that two laureates (MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero) are the cleaner configuration and that Bistritzer is the awkward one; if the committee comes to B054 in a few years, I would favour that shape. For this year the lattice clock has a settled, cross-checked interpretation.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B026 (the Higgs boson at ATLAS and CMS) first, arguing that the 2013 theory prize left an experimental gap and that the discovery is fully mature, while admitting leadership roles are an uncertain proxy for decisive credit.
responses.response: I accept the physics case: the Higgs discovery is a decisive, mature and independently confirmed result. My difficulty is attribution rather than worthiness. With two collaborations of thousands, naming three leaders risks crediting roles rather than the discovery, and you yourself flag that you are relying on memory for those roles. Outside particle physics I defer to you and Pearce on how the committee has handled such cases historically. If the committee is willing to resolve that question, I would regard B026 as a serious competitor, though I would not move it above B042 myself.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues treat optical lattice clocks as a distinct new regime or as an incremental step after the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether the formal redefinition of the second, or thorium-229 and ion-clock results, would make a later configuration more natural than Katori and Ye.
Whether a configuration with a second distinct achievement is needed given the three-person limit; I cannot see a natural second part that fits.
Whether the committee can settle the attribution disputes for B007 and B026 to a standard comparable to the clean Katori and Ye pairing.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B042 (optical lattice clocks) from my profile. I would flag that I direct WACQT and work at Chalmers MC2 in superconducting quantum circuits, and that I have a personal collaboration in phonon and artificial-atom work that touches B023 (optomechanics, Cleland); I would recuse myself from any configuration that includes B023. I have no known connection to Katori or Ye.
